title: Theatre skin preparation, hand decontamination and who checks the standard
audience: Operating-theatre clinical staff, theatre co-ordinators and operational managers, and cleaning contractors who need to know which parts of the theatre standards apply to their work.
learningOutcomes: Describe the hand decontamination requirement before a procedure, and the basis for choosing an alcohol or water-based skin preparation.
Explain how theatre co-ordinators and operational managers check the cleanliness standard.
Separate the parts of this lesson that apply to cleaning work from those that apply only to clinicians.

instruction.heading: Hand decontamination
instruction.body: The operating-theatre paper treats hand cleaning as a major way to cut infection, and asks that hands be cleaned using a suitable technique. The theatre protocol names the method, and the learner guide hand hygiene rules apply throughout (see “Hand cleaning: when to do it and which product fits”). Alcohol-based rub does not work on visibly dirty hands, so wash using soap and water first in that case. The surgical hand scrub is a clinical task and is not described further here.

instruction.heading: Skin preparation
instruction.body: According to that paper, alcohol mixtures outperform water mixtures for preparing skin, so alcohol is the favoured choice. The alcohol needs to air dry completely before work goes on. Skin preparation is a clinical task for theatre staff. Cleaning contractors do not prepare patient skin and must not touch a prepared site.

instruction.heading: Standards and audits
instruction.body: Co-ordinators carry the duty to verify cleanliness expectations and to act when they slip. It makes theatre operational managers responsible for regular audits of the standards, with a written record. The learner guide makes the employer responsible for policies and training, and each worker responsible for following them and reporting breaches to a supervisor. Where the two sources overlap, the facility written role descriptions decide.

instruction.heading: What cleaning contractors take from this lesson
instruction.body: Work only to the written instruction for each area that the co-ordinator provides. Report any standard that is not being met to the co-ordinator. Keep the audit records and checklists as the co-ordinator asks, and do not alter them.

instruction.heading: Parts of the theatre document not used
instruction.body: The theatre document includes a passage on post-mortem workers. That setting is outside this course and is not used. Its references to a trust waste policy and to a clinical waste section are UK-style, do not apply in Australia, and the clinical waste section is empty in the source. Waste rules come from “Clinical waste: segregation, containers and handling” and from state or territory law.

procedure: Before a procedure, carry out hand decontamination by the method the theatre protocol names.
Clinical staff: apply the skin preparation solution the protocol names, and allow it to dry before the procedure continues.
Co-ordinator: check the cleanliness standard against the written list for each theatre, and note any gap.
Operational manager: audit the theatre standards on the set schedule, and keep the written record.
Any worker: report a gap to the co-ordinator, and record the report.

workedExamples.situation: A theatre audit finds a cleaning checklist unsigned for three days.
workedExamples.reasoning: The co-ordinator must make sure the standard is met or start action. The audit record should show the finding, and the supervisor should explain why the checklist was not completed. The individual worker reports the reason if asked.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner asks whether they may prepare a patient skin before a procedure.
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Skin preparation is a clinical task under the theatre protocol. The cleaner keeps the surrounding area clean as the co-ordinator instructs.

equipmentAndPpe: Hand hygiene products listed by the facility
Audit checklist and written standards for each theatre
Gloves and eye protection for cleaning tasks, as the plan lists

commonErrors.error: Using an alcohol rub on visibly dirty hands.
commonErrors.prevention: Wash first using soap and water whenever hands look dirty.

commonErrors.error: Treating an audit as a replacement for the daily clean.
commonErrors.prevention: Audits check standards. The daily clean still has to be done.

commonErrors.error: Applying a UK trust policy as if it were Australian law.
commonErrors.prevention: Use state or territory law and the facility policy.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Skin preparation is a clinical task. Cleaning contractors do not prepare patient skin.
Completing this lesson does not grant a licence, certificate or authority to perform regulated work.

qualityStandard: Learner states the hand decontamination requirement and the rule for visibly soiled hands.
Learner explains the co-ordinator and operational manager roles in checking standards.
Learner separates cleaning-contractor content from clinician content in this lesson.
documentationEvidence: Audit record with date, theatre, findings and actions.
Co-ordinator report of any gap, with the time and the response.
summary: Hands are decontaminated by the theatre protocol method, and visibly soiled hands are washed first.
Co-ordinators make sure standards are met, and operational managers audit and record them.
Skin preparation is a clinical task, and the theatre sources that are UK-style or post-mortem are not used.

knowledgeChecks.question: Who must check the theatre cleanliness standards by regular audit?
Which statement about alcohol and water mixtures for skin preparation matches the operating-theatre paper?
options: Water-based solutions are better for dry skin and need no drying time
Alcohol solutions are preferred and must dry thoroughly before the procedure continues
Skin should be dried with a cloth before any alcohol is applied and the cloth must be sterile
Preparation is done by the cleaning contractor without any clinical staff present

knowledgeChecks.question: How should a cleaner read the paper reference to trust-level waste rules?
options: As a binding Australian rule for every theatre, every day, every shift and every clean
As a UK-style reference that does not apply here, so state, territory and facility rules govern
As a replacement for the learner guide for all cleaning staff in every facility
As a reason to skip waste sorting when the bins are already full of mixed waste today
